title: Writing With Machines and Peers: Designing for Critical Engagement with Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students engage with generative AI and peer feedback during an academic writing task, and how they develop reflective relationships with both human and AI reviewers. The authors are motivated by the rapid uptake of generative AI in education and the need for pedagogical designs that support critical, rather than superficial, AI use. They focus specifically on the writing process, asking how students incorporate AI and peer feedback across multiple revisions and how they make sense of these interactions.

The intervention was an 8-week pedagogical design in a graduate-level educational technologies course. Students completed a literature or landscape review project through several stages: initial drafting, AI review using a custom rubric-aligned tool called CyberScholar, revision, structured peer review, further revision, and written reflection. The AI tool provided automated rubric-based feedback and supported follow-up dialogue, while peers provided annotations and holistic rubric-based comments. The study used a case study mixed-methods design combining platform log data, writing drafts, peer reviews, automated textual revision analysis, and student reflections.

The population consisted of 10 consenting students from a graduate-level course at a large research university in the United States; most were doctoral students in social science-related fields. The context was a single course delivered through the CGScholar learning management system. The setting was effectively blended, with online platform-based writing and review activities alongside synchronous class discussions and peer feedback sessions.

The main conclusions are that students used AI and peer feedback in different but complementary ways. AI was especially useful for fast, structured, rubric-aligned guidance and surface-level improvements such as organization, grammar, and checking assignment expectations. Peer feedback was perceived as more context-sensitive, conceptually rich, and helpful for disciplinary relevance and higher-order argument development. Students varied substantially in depth of AI engagement: some used it transactionally as a scoring/checklist tool, while others engaged critically through dialogue. Overall, the authors argue that combining AI and peer feedback can support writing development, AI literacy, and critical human-AI collaboration when embedded in intentional pedagogy.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods single-course case study in higher education with descriptive quantitative logs and qualitative analysis, not a randomized trial or quasi-experiment. It has a clear methodology but no causal identification, control group, or outcome statistics suitable for effect-size synthesis.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests beneficial but qualitatively assessed impacts on writing development and critical AI engagement, with no credible standardized effect size or comparative impact estimate. Impact is therefore positive but unclear in magnitude and not directly generalizable to K-12 populations.

interventions.use_case: Custom GenAI reviewer (CyberScholar/CyberReview) providing rubric-aligned automated feedback and follow-up chat on graduate students’ academic literature review drafts.
Conversational interaction with GPT-4o/LLaMA-based reviewer to clarify feedback, ask follow-up questions, and discuss revision decisions during academic writing.
AI-assisted support for academic writing revision, including grammar, coherence, rubric alignment, and source/theory elaboration in literature review writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative and descriptive evidence that students used AI and peer feedback to revise graduate-level academic writing across multiple drafts, with different functions for each feedback source. Automated text-similarity metrics and case analyses suggest writing development and revision uptake, but no standardized writing outcome, inferential test, or effect size is reported; findings are based on 10 consenting students in one graduate course.
finding.measure: Revision trajectories across three draft versions, rubric-aligned feedback uptake, student writing artifacts, peer comments, and reflections on writing development

finding.finding_summary: The study finds students developed critical engagement with AI, reflective judgment about feedback sources, and strategic integration of AI versus peer input during writing. Evidence comes from chat logs, reflections, and two illustrative cases showing variation from deep to shallow engagement, but no validated durable-skills instrument or quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Coded AI interaction patterns (planning/ideation, information seeking and evaluation, writing/presentation, conversational engagement), written reflections, and thematic analysis of revision decisions

finding.finding_summary: Reflections suggest students reported increasing confidence and comfort using AI, but also frustration with generic, rigid, or overly long feedback and preference for peer encouragement in ambiguous situations. These findings indicate mixed affective responses rather than a tested improvement in motivation or engagement, and no scale-based statistics are provided.
finding.measure: Student reflections on confidence, encouragement, frustration, and perceived relationship with AI and peer reviewers
